analysis.one_liner: Makes federal civil asset forfeiture go through court with higher proof and stops agencies from keeping seized property.
analysis.headline: A House committee voted 26-0 to advance limits on civil asset forfeiture in June 2023, but the bill never got a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, federal agencies can seize cash, cars, and homes through civil asset forfeiture without charging the owner with a crime, and the owner has to prove their property is innocent to get it back. This bill would force every forfeiture through a federal court, raise the government's proof standard from 'preponderance of the evidence' to 'clear and convincing evidence,' provide a lawyer for poor owners whose home is seized, and require a hearing within 14 days when cash is seized on suspicion of 'structuring' bank deposits. It would also stop agencies from keeping the proceeds: forfeited property would go to the Treasury's general fund instead of the Justice Department's forfeiture fund, and the program that lets federal agencies share seizure money with state and local police would be eliminated.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary property owners who have cash, vehicles, or homes seized by federal agencies without being convicted of any crime. Indigent owners facing forfeiture of their primary residence would get appointed counsel. People whose cash is seized over alleged structuring would get a court hearing within 14 days, and the property would be returned unless the court finds probable cause. The changes would also apply to forfeiture cases already pending.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Owners whose property was seized without charges

how_it_helps.text: Raises the government's burden of proof in civil forfeiture from a preponderance of the evidence to clear and convincing evidence, and requires the government to show a substantial connection between the property and an offense [S2, S3].
Ends nonjudicial (administrative) forfeiture: no federal seizing agency could forfeit property on its own, and every forfeiture order would have to come from a United States district court [S2, S3].
Requires appointed counsel for an indigent owner whose primary residence is subject to a civil forfeiture hearing [S2].

Eliminates statutory authority for equitable sharing and directs forfeiture proceeds into the Treasury general fund instead of the DOJ Assets Forfeiture Fund, removing the financial incentive agencies have to seize property [S2, S3].

For cash seized in structuring cases, requires a probable-cause hearing within 14 days of notice and returns the property unless the court finds probable cause, and adds a 'knowingly' requirement to structuring offenses [S2, S3].
Requires courts to weigh factors like the seriousness of the offense, the property's connection to it, its value, and hardship to the owner before allowing a forfeiture [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal law-enforcement agencies, including the Justice Department, which currently draw money and equipment from the DOJ Assets Forfeiture Fund, and state and local police departments that receive 'equitable sharing' payments of federal forfeiture proceeds. Defense counsel appointments for indigent homeowners would add court costs. The strongest objection supporters would have to answer is that the bill weakens a tool used to take proceeds from drug trafficking organizations.

drawbacks.text: Law enforcement argues forfeiture is a key tool for dismantling drug trafficking organizations, and that raising the proof standard, requiring court proceedings, and ending administrative forfeitures would make it harder to strip criminals of illegal proceeds [S2].

Eliminating the DOJ Assets Forfeiture Fund and equitable sharing ends a funding stream that currently pays for some law-enforcement programs and shared grants, shifting costs to regular appropriations [S2, S3].
Appointing counsel for indigent homeowners and running every case through district court adds expenses and time to the forfeiture process [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For property owners the gains are real: they would no longer have to litigate to get back seized property under a low proof standard, and the profit motive behind seizures would be removed. The main cost falls on law enforcement, which loses a revenue stream and a streamlined seizure tool. The bill leaves criminal forfeiture intact, so convicted criminals could still lose property; the changes mainly protect people never charged with a crime. The tradeoff favors owners, though agencies' warnings about slower asset recovery in organized-crime cases are a fair point.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee voted 26-0 to advance the bill in June 2023, but no further action followed and the bill never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 9, 2023 by Rep. Tim Walberg with original cosponsors from both parties: Reps. Raskin, McClintock, Neguse, Armstrong, and Cardenas [S3, S5].
It was referred to four committees: Judiciary, plus Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Financial Services [S5].
On June 14, 2023, the House Judiciary Committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported in the nature of a substitute (amended) by a vote of 26-0 [S5].

After the committee vote, no further action was taken: the bill was never reported to the floor, never received a House vote, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without either chamber voting on it [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal law-enforcement agencies and state and local police departments that collect forfeiture proceeds under current law; the status quo, where agencies keep what they seize without a conviction, continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law-enforcement agencies that keep seizure proceeds

for.name: Rep. Tim Walberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited bipartisan original cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. Jamie Raskin, Tom McClintock, Joe Neguse, Kelly Armstrong, and Tony Cardenas
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.role: Committee with primary jurisdiction over forfeiture law
for.what_they_did: Held a markup on June 14, 2023 and voted 26-0 to order the bill reported amended.

against.name: House leadership / Office of the Speaker
against.role: Controls which reported bills get floor time
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote after the committee reported it; the action history shows no floor action after June 14, 2023.

against.name: Law-enforcement agencies reliant on forfeiture revenue
against.role: DOJ Assets Forfeiture Fund beneficiaries and state/local police in equitable-sharing programs
against.what_they_did: The bill would have eliminated the funding streams these agencies draw from forfeited property; they are the concentrated interest the status quo protects.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican, the original cosponsors split evenly across both parties, and the Judiciary Committee advanced it 26-0 with no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Federal law-enforcement agencies (DOJ Assets Forfeiture Fund)
industries.note: The bill ends these agencies' ability to conduct nonjudicial forfeitures and redirects proceeds from their own fund to the Treasury general fund. Under current law the same agencies that seize property keep the proceeds, which is the financial incentive the bill removes.

industries.industry: State and local police departments receiving equitable-sharing payments
industries.note: The bill eliminates statutory authority for equitable sharing, the program through which local police receive a share of federal forfeiture proceeds. This is the mechanism most criticized for encouraging policing for profit, because local departments can share in federal seizures even when state law would not allow it.

Requiring judicial process for every forfeiture and appointed counsel for indigent homeowners routes more cases through federal courts and expands appointed-representation work. This is a minor effect compared to the bill's core purpose.
